query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) into a high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating will promote the in-situ formation of a lubricious MoO2 layer during friction, thereby simultaneously reducing the friction coefficient and wear rate over a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy or HEA coating (e.g., (AlCrTiZr)N-based system) without Mo, which exhibits standard friction and wear characteristics under sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a predetermined molybdenum content into the HEA formulation during deposition (e.g., via multi-target co-deposition magnetron sputtering) to form a modified (AlCrTiZrMox)N alloy coating.
generation.conditions: Ambient or moderate-oxygen environments and sliding conditions across a broad service-temperature range (from room temperature to elevated temperatures) where frictional heating can trigger localized oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo-enriched coating develops a columnar microstructure that, upon friction-induced heating, facilitates localized oxidation of Mo to form a thin, self-lubricating MoO2 layer.
generation.mechanism: During friction, the shear and localized heat promote oxidation of the incorporated Mo. MoO2 forms a layered, easy-shear tribolayer that both reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and lowers the shear forces at the sliding interface, while the improved hardness and toughness of the modified coating help to retard wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Mo-incorporated HEA coating is expected to reduce the friction coefficient by a factor of approximately 2–3 and lower the wear rate by up to an order of magnitude, maintaining these improvements across the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (friction coefficient and wear rate) of the standard HEA coating without Mo under identical sliding and thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective as long as the oxide-forming conditions are met (i.e., sufficient frictional heat and oxygen availability). Extreme environments that prevent Mo oxidation or cause rapid degradation of the oxide layer (e.g., very low oxygen or corrosive atmospheres that dissolve MoO2) might limit its effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements and long-term stability of the lubricious oxide film under variable load and speed conditions remain to be determined. Uncertainty also exists regarding the optimal Mo concentration that maximizes lubrication without compromising other mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one set with the Mo addition (e.g., (AlCrTiZrMox)N with optimized Mo content) and a control set without Mo. Subject both sets to standardized ball‐on‐disk sliding tests under controlled loads and sliding speeds, over a temperature range (room temperature up to the high service temperature). Monitor friction coefficients and wear rates continuously during the tests.
measurements: Real-time friction coefficient via high-resolution tribometer
Wear volume and wear rate via profilometry or weight-loss measurements
Surface analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS, XRD) to confirm the presence and continuity of the MoO2 lubricious layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Mo-incorporated coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control samples, or if surface analyses do not confirm the formation of a continuous, lubricious MoO2 layer during friction.

cited_evidence.text: As is well known, friction between components is the main cause of the failure of mechanical equipment under extreme conditions, such as high speed and high temperature [,]. Based on the data on global energy consumption and economic expenditure, energy losses related to friction-and-wear account for one-third of global energy consumption [,]. Traditionally, the way to reduce friction is usually to use oil or grease lubrication systems []. However, some devices with high cleanliness requirements do not allow the presence of foreign additives such as lubricating oil. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate new materials and lubricating media to reduce friction and wear.
